resources.string: Traps
Common mistakes
Summary
right
wrong
Right: %1$s
Wrong: %1$s
4. All nullable: ε goes in. Repeat until stable.
Step four: if every symbol of the rule is nullable, epsilon goes in. Then repeat it all, until a round changes nothing.
FIRST(S) = { a, ε, c }, because A starts with a or vanishes.
A classmate computed FIRST of S like this. Is it right or wrong? Tap.
A is nullable, but after it comes b, which never vanishes.
Epsilon goes in only if the whole rule can vanish. Here b always stays, so b is what goes in.
FIRST(S) = { a, b, c }. The ε from A does not carry over to S.
Stopping at the first nonterminal even when it is nullable.
If it is nullable, also add FIRST of the next symbol.
Another common mistake is stopping early. A nullable nonterminal does not close the computation: look at the symbol after it.
FIRST(α): the terminals that can start what α generates.
ε goes in only when everything in α is nullable.
Repeat the steps until a round changes nothing.
To sum up: FIRST is the set of possible starts. Epsilon goes in only when everything can vanish. And the computation repeats until nothing changes.
4. Repeat until a round changes nothing.
Step four: one FOLLOW depends on another. Repeat the steps until a whole round adds nothing.
FOLLOW(F) = { *, ε }, because Y comes after F.
A classmate copied all of FIRST of Y into FOLLOW of F. Right or wrong? Tap.
FOLLOW holds only terminals and the dollar sign.
Correct. Epsilon never goes into FOLLOW. When Y vanishes, what goes in is FOLLOW of T.
FOLLOW(F) = { *, +, ), $ }. There is never ε in FOLLOW.
Forgetting $ in FOLLOW of the start symbol.
The start symbol always has $ in its FOLLOW.
Another mistake is forgetting the dollar sign. Without it, the rule that vanishes at the end of input has no column in the table.
FOLLOW(B): the terminals that can come right after B.
It comes from FIRST of what follows B. If that vanishes, from FOLLOW of the left-hand side.
It never has ε. The start symbol always has $.
To sum up: FOLLOW is what can come after. It comes from FIRST of the neighbor and from FOLLOW of whoever is left of the arrow. Epsilon never goes in.
The rule R → ε goes into the FOLLOW(R) columns of the LL(1) table.
A classmate said where the vanishing rule goes. Right or wrong? Tap.
Nobody reads epsilon. The vanishing rule is used when the next token may come after R.
R vanishes when the next token may come after it, and those tokens are the FOLLOW of R. There is no epsilon column.
Checking only FIRST to say the grammar is LL(1).
A nullable rule takes the FOLLOW and may clash with FIRST of another.
A common mistake is checking FIRST only. A nullable rule takes the FOLLOW columns, and there it may clash with another rule.
Row: nonterminal. Column: terminal or $.
A → α goes under FIRST(α). If α is nullable, also under FOLLOW(A).
Two rules in a cell: conflict. Empty cell: syntax error.
To sum up: the table stores, for each nonterminal and each token, the rule to use. FIRST fills almost everything. FOLLOW handles the rules that vanish.
To replace E with T X, I push X first and then T.
In what order does the right-hand side go onto the stack? A classmate did this. Right or wrong?
Whatever must be read first has to end up on top. Which of the two is it?
Push back to front: first X, then T. That way T is on top and is handled first.
Advancing the input when using X → ε.
Only X leaves the stack. The token stays in the input.
A common mistake: advancing the input when applying a rule. Only matching a terminal consumes a token. Replacing by epsilon just pops the top.
The stack starts with $ and the start symbol.
Nonterminal on top: replace by the table. Terminal on top: match the token.
$ with $ accepts. Empty cell or different terminal is an error.
To sum up: the predictive parser looks at the top and one token. The table picks the rule, matching consumes input, and dollar with dollar accepts.
E → E + T becomes: void E() { E(); match('+'); T(); }
A classmate translated a left-recursive rule straight into code. Right or wrong?
Look at the first thing function E does, before reading any token.
E calls E without consuming anything, and the recursion never ends. Before descending, remove the left recursion.
Left recursion hangs the descent. Remove it first: E → T X.
Handling the ε rule with a call match(ε).
The ε rule is the empty else: the function returns without consuming a token.
Another mistake is trying to match epsilon. Epsilon is not a token. The epsilon rule is just returning without doing anything.
Each nonterminal is a function. A nonterminal in a rule is a call; a terminal is match.
The if looks at the next token and picks the rule by FIRST.
Only for LL(1) grammars: no left recursion, left-factored.
To sum up: recursive descent is the predictive parser as code. One function per nonterminal, one if per rule, and the call stack plays the role of the stack.
In panic mode, the parser fixes the program and generates the code.
What does recovery deliver in the end? A classmate said this. Right or wrong?
It threw tokens away. What is left is no longer your program.
Recovery is there to find more errors. With a syntax error, the compiler generates no code.
Recovery only serves to report more errors in the same compilation.
Synchronizing on whatever token shows up.
Synchronize on FIRST or FOLLOW of the top, like the ; that closes the statement.
Another mistake is to stop discarding too early. On an arbitrary token, the parser gets stuck again and prints cascading errors that are not even real.
Error: empty table cell, or terminal on top different from the token.
Panic mode: discard up to a synchronizing token (FIRST or FOLLOW of the top).
Goal: report several errors at once, with no cascading errors.
To sum up: on an error, the parser reports, discards up to a safe token and goes on. FOLLOW gives the safe tokens. The goal is to show every error in one compilation.
Every rule right-hand side on top of the stack is a handle.
Whenever the top matches a right-hand side, do I reduce? Right or wrong? Tap.
Think of id plus id times id. With E plus T on top and times in the input, reducing ruins the computation.
It is a handle only if the reduction leads back to the start symbol. Sometimes shifting more is right, and the table decides.
A handle is the right-hand side whose reduction is part of the rightmost derivation.
Looking for a handle in the middle of the stack.
The handle always shows up on top. The parser never touches the middle.
Another mistake: looking for a handle in the middle of the stack. In shift-reduce, the handle always forms on top.
Shift: the token goes on top. Reduce: the handle becomes the left-hand side.
Accept with only the start symbol on the stack and $ in the input.
The reductions, read backwards, give the rightmost derivation.
To sum up: shift-reduce reads first and decides later. It shifts until a handle forms on top, reduces, and repeats until only the start symbol is left.
In the closure, the rules of every symbol after the dot go in, terminal or not.
When does the closure pull in new rules? A classmate said this. Right or wrong?
A terminal has no rules. Only a nonterminal does.
The closure only acts when the dot is right before a nonterminal. And only the symbol right after the dot counts.
Closure: only for the nonterminal right after the dot.
Moving the dot in the goto and forgetting the closure.
Every goto ends with a closure. Without it, the state is missing items.
Another mistake: moving the dot and stopping. If the new dot is before a nonterminal, its rules go into the state.
Item: a rule with a dot. Before it has been read; after it is still expected.
Closure pulls in rules; goto moves the dot and closes. Each set is a state.
A dot at the end is a complete item: a sign to reduce.
To sum up: the item marks progress in a rule. Closure and goto build the states, and the complete item signals the reduction.
State with A → α •: I write r in every column.
Where does the reduction go in the SLR table? A classmate filled it in like this. Right or wrong?
That is what LR(0) does. SLR checks a set first.
Exactly. In SLR, the reduction goes only into the columns of FOLLOW of A. Filling the whole row creates conflicts that are not there.
In SLR, r goes only into the columns of FOLLOW(A).
Writing s (shift) in a nonterminal's column.
A nonterminal's column is the GOTO part: just the state number.
Another mistake: putting a shift in a nonterminal's column. Nobody reads a nonterminal from the input. Only the target state, the goto, goes there.
Terminal after the dot: s (shift) and go to the goto state.
Complete item A → α •: r in the columns of FOLLOW(A).
Two actions in one cell: conflict. With no conflict, the grammar is SLR(1).
To sum up: the SLR table comes from the LR(0) automaton and FOLLOW. Gotos become shifts, complete items become reduces under FOLLOW, and an empty cell is an error.
Every LALR(1) grammar is LR(1), but not every LR(1) grammar is LALR(1).
Are LALR and LR(1) equally strong? A classmate said this. Right or wrong?
Merging states with the same core can mix lookaheads that LR(1) kept apart.
You got it. The merge can create a reduce-reduce conflict that LR(1) did not have. That is why LALR sits between SLR and LR(1).
Using FOLLOW to fill in the reductions of the LALR table.
In LALR, the reduction goes into the columns of the item's lookaheads.
A common mistake: using FOLLOW in LALR. FOLLOW belongs to SLR. In LALR and LR(1), the item's lookahead decides the column.
LR(1) item: rule, dot and lookahead.
LALR: merge LR(1) states with equal cores and union the lookaheads.
Size of SLR, power between SLR and LR(1). It is Bison's method.
To sum up: LR(1) keeps the lookahead in each item. LALR merges states with the same core. It is as small as SLR and almost as strong as LR(1).
In Bison, the precedence line that comes last binds tightest.
The order of the precedence lines matters. A classmate said this. Right or wrong?
In the calculator, times was declared after plus, and times binds tighter.
The last line has the highest precedence. That is why times comes after plus.
Ignoring the conflict warning because the parser was generated.
An unhandled conflict is Bison choosing for you. Use %left or rewrite the rule.
A common mistake: ignoring the conflict warning. The parser comes out, but Bison's default choice may build the wrong tree.
The .y file: declarations, %%, and the rules with their actions.
$$ is the value of the left-hand side; $1, $2 and $3 are those of the right-hand side.
%left and %right resolve conflicts. The last line has higher precedence.
To sum up: Bison generates the LALR table from the dot y file. Actions compute values at reduction, and precedence lines resolve the conflicts.
A variable used without being declared is a semantic error: the sentence has the right form.
Which phase catches this error? A classmate answered this. Right or wrong?
The grammar accepts the statement even without the declaration. Who checks what the name means?
Syntax analysis only looks at the form. Knowing whether the name was declared is the job of semantic analysis.
The compiler runs the program.
The compiler only translates. The processor runs it, or an interpreter does.
A common mistake: thinking the compiler runs the program. It only translates. An interpreter is what runs it directly, without generating the file.
Analysis: lexical → tokens; syntax → tree; semantic → typed tree.
Synthesis: intermediate code, optimization and code generation.
Lexical error: character. Syntax: form. Semantic: meaning.
To sum up: the compiler translates in six phases. Three analyze the source code, three build the machine code. Each phase catches one kind of error.
For x>=10, the scanner produces the tokens x, >, = and 10.
How does the scanner cut this piece? A classmate cut it like this. Right or wrong?
The scanner always takes the longest piece that forms a token.
By longest match, greater-or-equal is a single token. That makes three tokens, not four.
x>=10 gives three tokens: x, >= and 10. That is longest match.
Token and lexeme are the same thing.
The lexeme is the text (total2). The token carries the class (ID) and the lexeme.
Another mistake: mixing up token and lexeme. The lexeme is the text that was in the file. The token is what the parser receives: the class, with the lexeme attached.
The scanner reads characters and hands tokens to the parser.
Longest match: always the longest piece that forms a token.
The lexeme is the text; the token carries the class and the lexeme. Spaces and comments vanish.
To sum up: lexical analysis turns characters into tokens. It uses longest match, tells lexeme from class and throws away spaces and comments.
The string went through a final state along the way, so it was accepted.
When does the automaton accept? A classmate said this. Right or wrong?
What matters is where the train is when the string ends.
Only the state where reading ends counts. Passing through a final state midway accepts nothing.
Accept only if the whole string was read and it stopped in a final state.
The expression a* requires at least one a.
The star accepts zero times. For one or more, use a a* (or a+).
Another mistake: thinking the star requires at least one repetition. Star means zero or more. The empty string matches too.
The regular expression describes the format; the automaton checks it.
DFA: one initial state, one arrow per symbol in each state, final states.
Accept if it read everything and stopped in a final state. No transition: reject.
To sum up: the regular expression describes a token's format, and the finite automaton checks string by string. Accepting means finishing the reading in a final state.
The set {0, 2} is final in the DFA if 0 or 2 is final in the NFA.
When is a set final in the DFA? A classmate said this. Right or wrong?
The NFA accepts if some path reaches a final state. Does it have to be all of them?
One final state inside the set is enough. The NFA accepts when at least one path works out.
Computing move and forgetting the ε-closure of the result.
After each move, apply the ε-closure. Otherwise states are missing.
A common mistake: forgetting the epsilon closure after reading the symbol. The states reached by epsilon are part of the set too.
Each DFA state is a set of NFA states.
Start at the ε-closure of the initial state. For each symbol: move, then ε-closure.
A set with some final state is final. It ends when no new set appears.
To sum up: the subset construction walks with all possible states at once. Each set becomes a DFA state, and one final state inside is enough to accept.
A and B go to different states with b. So A and B are different.
Is it enough for the targets to be different states to mark the pair? Right or wrong?
What if the two targets are equivalent to each other?
I mark the pair only if the targets form an already marked pair. Targets that differ but are equivalent separate nobody.
Mark the pair only when the targets form an already marked pair.
Stopping after the first round of targets.
Repeat until a whole round marks no pair.
Another mistake: stopping early. A new mark can reveal another difference. Finish only when a round goes by blank.
Equivalent states accept and reject the same continuations.
Mark final with non-final. Then the pairs that go to marked pairs.
Pairs left unmarked at the end are equivalent: merge them.
To sum up: minimization separates what is different and merges what is left. It starts with final against non-final, propagates along the transitions and stops when nothing changes.
In Flex, the longest match wins. The order of the rules only breaks ties.
Which one wins when two rules match? A classmate said this. Right or wrong?
Remember ifa: which rule won, the upper one or the longer one?
That's it. ifa matches whole as a name, which is longer than if. Only on a tie in length does the upper rule win.
Putting the identifier rule before the reserved words.
Reserved words first. Otherwise while and if become ID.
A common mistake: putting the identifier rule on top. Then if and while tie on length, lose on order and become ordinary names.
The .l file: pattern (regular expression) and action in C.
The longest match wins; on a tie, the upper rule.
An action with no return discards the text. That is how spaces vanish.
To sum up: Flex generates the scanner from patterns and actions. The longest wins, order breaks ties, and reserved words go on top.
In a leftmost derivation, I may replace any nonterminal at each step.
A classmate described the leftmost derivation like this. Right or wrong? Tap.
The name says which nonterminal gets replaced.
At each step, the leftmost nonterminal is always the one replaced. In a rightmost derivation, always the rightmost.
Leftmost: always replace the first nonterminal of the form.
Replacing a terminal by a rule.
Only a nonterminal goes on the left-hand side. A terminal is a token and does not change.
Another mistake: trying to replace a terminal. A terminal is a token and has no rule. Only a nonterminal goes on the left-hand side of a production.
Grammar: terminals, nonterminals, productions and a start symbol.
Deriving: start at the start symbol and replace nonterminals until only terminals are left.
The sentence is in the language if a derivation for it exists.
To sum up: a context-free grammar generates sentences by replacements. Deriving is applying productions from the start symbol, and the tree records those replacements.
I found two different derivations for the sentence. So the grammar is ambiguous.
Do two different derivations of the same sentence prove ambiguity? Right or wrong?
The leftmost and the rightmost derivations can draw the same tree.
What counts is two different trees, or two leftmost derivations. Just changing the order of the replacements proves nothing.
Ambiguous: one sentence with two trees, or two leftmost derivations.
I tested three sentences, each gave one tree. So it is not ambiguous.
Examples do not prove there is no ambiguity. One counterexample proves there is.
Another mistake: concluding the grammar is unambiguous because a few sentences gave a single tree. Only a counterexample proves anything, and it proves ambiguity.
Ambiguity: some sentence has two parse trees.
To prove it, show one sentence and the two trees.
The fix: one level per precedence, and recursion on the side of the associativity.
To sum up: an ambiguous grammar gives two trees for the same sentence, and two trees are two computations. You fix it with precedence levels and recursion on the right side.
To remove the recursion from A → A α | β, just write A → α A | β.
A classmate fixed the left recursion like this. Right or wrong? Tap.
Generate a sentence with both versions. Does beta end up at the start or at the end?
The original generates beta followed by several alphas. The classmate's generates the alphas before beta. The language changed.
A → β A' and A' → α A' | ε. The β stays at the start.
Forgetting ε in the new rule A'.
Without A' → ε the repetition never ends, and no sentence is generated.
Another mistake: forgetting epsilon in A prime. It is what ends the repetition. Without it, the derivation never reaches terminals only.
Left recursion: A → A α. The top-down parser loops forever.
The fix: A → β A' and A' → α A' | ε.
The language does not change; the tree does. The parser's loop keeps the arithmetic right.
To sum up: left recursion hangs a top-down parser. The fix puts beta in front and pushes the repetition into a new nonterminal, which ends with epsilon.
Factoring A → a b | a c does not change the sentences the grammar generates.
Does left factoring change the language? A classmate said this. Right or wrong?
Derive a b and a c with the factored grammar. Does any new sentence come out?
That's it. A → a A' and A' → b | c generate a b and a c, the same sentences. Factoring only changes when the choice is made.
Factoring out only part of the common prefix.
Use the longest common prefix, and repeat if equal starts remain.
A common mistake: factoring halfway. If the new alternatives still start the same, the conflict remains. Repeat until no common prefix is left.
Common prefix: two alternatives of the same nonterminal start the same way.
Factoring: A → α A', and A' gets the rest of each alternative.
It does not change the language. It is one of the preparations for an LL(1) grammar.
To sum up: a common prefix prevents choosing with one token. Factoring pulls the prefix out and postpones the decision, without changing the language.
A synthesized attribute is the one a node receives from its parent.
Where does a synthesized attribute come from? A classmate said this. Right or wrong?
In this lesson, did the types go up or down the tree?
Synthesized goes up: the node computes it from its children. What comes from the parent or the siblings is an inherited attribute.
Synthesized: computed from the children. Inherited: comes from the parent or the siblings.
int + float is a type error.
There is coercion: the int becomes float. Mixing bool with a number is the error.
Another mistake: treating every mix of types as an error. Integer with real has coercion. It is an error when no conversion makes sense.
Attribute: information on a tree node, computed by semantic rules.
The type is synthesized: it goes up from the leaves to the root.
int with float is coerced to float. No possible conversion: semantic error.

To sum up: semantic analysis annotates the tree with attributes. The type is a synthesized attribute, which goes up from the children. Along the way, the compiler applies coercion or reports an error.
With an x outside, I may declare another x in an inner block: the inner one hides the outer one.
There is already an x outside. May I declare another x inside the block? A classmate said this. Right or wrong?
The new declaration goes into the top table, which has no x yet.
In another scope it is fine. The inner x hides the outer one. Declaring twice in the same block is the error.
Looking the name up only in the top table.
The lookup goes from the top down to the global table. An error only if none has it.
A common mistake: searching only the current block. The lookup goes through every table on the stack, from the innermost block to the global one.
Symbol table: name, type and where each thing was declared.
One table per block, on a stack. Open a block, push; close it, pop.
Use: lookup from the top down. The innermost hides the outer one.
To sum up: the scope says where each declaration holds. The stack of symbol tables resolves each name, always from the innermost block to the outermost.
The AST of a * (b - 2) has no node for the parentheses.
Do parentheses appear in the AST? A classmate drew it without them. Right or wrong?
The parenthesis changes the shape of the tree. After that, is it still useful?
Nice. The parenthesis only groups. In the AST, the grouping is already in the shape: minus sits below times.
Putting at the root the first operator that appears in the expression.
The root holds the last operation to be computed.
A common mistake: putting the first operator of the line at the root. The root is the last operation. The first operation sits at the bottom of the tree.
Parse tree: one node per rule. AST: only operations and operands.
An operator becomes an inner node; names and values become leaves.
Parentheses and pass-through rules vanish. Deeper is computed earlier.
To sum up: the AST is the parse tree without what only serves the grammar. The operators, the operands and the order of operations remain.
x = a + b * c needs two three-address lines.
How many three-address lines does this assignment need? A classmate said this. Right or wrong?
Count the operators. Each line takes at most one.
Exactly. There are two operations: t1 = b * c, then x = a + t1. Each line takes one operator and at most three addresses.
Reusing the same temporary for two different operations.
Each operator gets a new temporary: t1, t2, t3...
A common mistake: reusing t1 in the second operation. If the old value is still needed, it gets lost. Each result gets a new temporary.
Three addresses: result = operand operator operand.
Generate the children before the parent; each operation stores into a new temporary.
It is intermediate code: it does not depend on the processor.
To sum up: three-address code breaks the expression into simple operations. The tree gives the order, and each partial result gets a temporary.
With x read from the keyboard, the compiler folds x * 2 into a number.
Can this operation be folded? A classmate said yes. Right or wrong?
Does the value of x exist yet at compile time?
The value of x only shows up when the program runs. Constant folding only applies to what the compiler already knows.
Only operations on constants known at compile time are folded.
Accepting an optimization that changes the result in some case.
A valid optimization gives the same result for every input.
Another mistake: thinking speed is worth changing the result in some rare case. It is not. An optimization must always preserve the result.
Optimizing: faster or smaller code, with the same result.
Constant folding: an operation on constants only is done at compile time.
With a variable, the operation is left for run time.
To sum up: optimization improves the code without changing what it does. Constant folding solves at compile time everything that does not depend on a variable.
In a recursion, each call has its own n, in its own activation record.
Where does the n of each call to fat live? A classmate said this. Right or wrong?
How many activation records were on the stack while fat of one was running?
You got it. Each call pushes a record with its own n. If there were only one, recursion would destroy the values.
Functions return in the order they were called.
It is a stack: the last call is the first to return.
A common mistake: thinking whoever was called first returns first. It is the opposite. The stack returns in the reverse order of the calls.
Activation record: parameters, local variables and return address.
A call pushes a record; a return pops it.
Only the record on top is executing.
To sum up: each call gets an activation record on the stack, with its parameters, its locals and the return address. The last call is the first to return.
To add a and b, just write: add a, b straight in memory.
In MIPS, can you add two variables straight in memory? A classmate wrote this. Right or wrong?
The MIPS add only takes registers.
That's it. First lw loads each variable into a register. Only then does add do the operation.
lw, lw, add, sw: the operation happens between registers only.
Ending at the add and forgetting the sw.
Without sw, the variable in memory keeps its old value.
Another mistake: stopping at the operation. The result is in the register, but the variable lives in memory. Without the sw, it does not change.
lw: from memory to register. sw: from register to memory.
add, sub and mul operate between registers only.
Each three-address line becomes: load, operate, store.
To sum up: generating code is translating each three-address line for the machine. In MIPS, that means loading with lw, operating between registers and storing with sw.
Four temporaries may fit into fewer than four registers.
How many registers does this code need? A classmate counted the temporaries. Right or wrong?
In the example, four temporaries fit into how many registers?
What counts is how many are live at the same time. Those that never coexist can share a register.
Computing liveness from top to bottom.
Liveness runs from bottom to top: live means still to be read.
A common mistake: computing liveness from top to bottom. Live means it will still be read later, so the analysis starts at the end.
Live: the value will still be read further down.
Interference graph: an edge between those live at the same time.
Coloring: neighbors with different colors. Out of colors: spill to memory.
To sum up: allocation decides who stays in a register. Liveness shows who coexists, the graph links those that coexist, and coloring hands out the registers.
Run the SLR table
state stack: %1$s
input: %1$s
shift, go to 2
reduce by rule 2
This is the full SLR table for the grammar E goes to E plus n, or n. The columns n, plus and dollar are the ACTION part. The column E is the GOTO part.
The parser keeps a stack of states, which starts with state zero. The action comes from the cell of the top state and the next token.
Top zero, token n. The cell says s2. What does the parser do? Tap.
The letter s comes from shift.
The n leaves the input, and state two goes onto the stack.
Now the top is two and the token is plus. The cell says r2: reduce by rule two, E goes to n. The right-hand side has one symbol, so one state is popped.
Zero is on top, and the reduction produced an E. Which cell gives the next state? Tap it.
Row of the state left on top, column of the reduced nonterminal.
Exactly. GOTO of zero with E is one, and state one goes onto the stack. Every reduction ends with a goto.
Top one, token plus: s3. Top three, token n: s4. The stack is now zero, one, three, four, and dollar is left in the input.
Top four, token dollar: r1, the rule E goes to E plus n. How many states are popped? Tap.
Count the symbols on the right-hand side of rule one.
Three symbols on the right-hand side, three states out. Zero is left, and GOTO of zero with E gives one again.
Top one, token dollar: the cell says ok. The input is accepted.
Shift pushes a state. Reduce pops one state per rule symbol and looks up GOTO.
if and while become jumps
label: L1:
jump: goto L1
nothing
So far, three-address code only did arithmetic. But programs have if and while, and the machine has neither.
The machine only knows how to go on to the next line or jump to a line marked with a label.
First the condition becomes an operation, stored in t1. Then comes the conditional jump: if t1 is false, jump to L1.
If the condition is true, execution goes on to the next line. Which statement goes there? Tap.
It is the statement that runs when a is less than b.
The if block comes right after the conditional jump.
After x equals one, what keeps execution from falling into the else? Tap.
With nothing there, the next line is the else.
Nice. An unconditional jump skips the else and goes to the end, at label L2.
Label L1 marks the start of the else. L2 marks the end of the whole if.
The while uses the same pieces. The label goes before the condition, and at the end of the body a goto goes back to it.
In the while, where does the goto at the end of the body go? Tap the line.
The loop has to test the condition again.
It goes back to the condition, which is tested on every pass.
if and while become three pieces: label, conditional jump and unconditional jump. That is how your loop reaches MIPS.
The type that goes down
goes up
goes down
records in the table
adds the values
S-attributed
L-attributed
In the declaration int a, b, the type is written only once, at the start. But a and b need it.
The type is born at node T, from the token int. That attribute is synthesized: it goes up from the child to T.
The a and the b are below L, which is a sibling of T. To reach them, does the type go up or down the tree? Tap.
The ids are leaves, down at the bottom. The type is up above.
It passes from T to its sibling L and goes down. An attribute that comes from the parent or a sibling is an inherited attribute.
The semantic rule says: the inherited attribute of L gets the type of T. At each lower L, the inherited value is copied from the L above.
